The Thirty Years War The devastation of the Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648) brought mixed fortune for the Jews of Prague. On the one hand, Emperor Ferdinand II, desperate for economic support in the war, took great pains to ensure the safety of the Jews. Although his troops ransacked Prague after the Battle of White Mountain, the emperor prohibited them from harming the Jewish Quarter and even had guards posted outside their homes. To the Jews of Prague, this was nothing short of a miracle. To commemorate this momentous event, they established the 14th of the Hebrew month of Cheshvan – the day the invasion began – as a Purim of Prague. The Jewish Cemetery of Prague The representative of Prague’s Jewish Community during the Thirty Years’ War was the financier Ya’akov Bassevi of Treuenburg (1570–1634). He was also the first Jew knighted in Europe. Yet, as his financial needs increased, Ferdinand II made the continuation of Jewish privilege dependent on the Jews’ paying higher taxes and on providing the emperor with a loan of 24,000 gulden. It was these tax requirements that, in 1627, led some resentful Jews to turn on their great Rabbi Yomtov Lipman Heller, who was forced out of Prague and eventually settled in Cracow. Difficult Times for the Jews of Prague After the Thirty Years’ War, measures were taken by the state authorities to reduce the number of Jews and to segregate them more strictly in a ghetto. Implementation of these measures was prevented in 1680 by an outbreak of plague, which took the lives of more than 3,500 Jews. To prevent further Jewish population growth, Emperor Charles VI (1711–1740) issued the cruel Familiants Law in 1726 and 1727. The Familiants Laws decreed that only 8,541 Jewish families would be tolerated in Bohemia and 5,106 in Moravia. Only the eldest son in a Jewish family would be given the right to marry. All other sons were forced to emigrate, try to marry illegally in the countryside, or die single. This would have a devastating effect on Bohemian Jewry for the next 120 years. This legislation remained in effect up to the Revolution of 1848. The position of the Jews under Emperor Charles VI was even worse when his daughter, Maria Theresa, became empress in 1740. Empress Maria Theresa, an ardent Catholic and antisemite, accused the Jews of siding with the Prussians during her battles for the “Hapsburg Heritage.” She decreed the expulsion of the Jews from Bohemia in 1744 and Moravia in 1745. Although the Prague City Council opposed the action, the Jews were forced out of Prague during a severe winter in January 1745. For a few years, they were permitted to remain in Bohemian villages at least two days’ distance from Prague. But Empress Maria Theresa had not counted on the devastating effect this would have on Prague’s economy. Jews had been moneylenders, suppliers of raw materials, and good customers in Prague markets. Without the Jews, the economy was in shambles. Interior of the Spanish Synagogue In 1748, the empress rescinded her decree, and Jews were permitted to return to Prague. To avoid humiliation, she imposed a severe annual “toleration tax” of 204,000 guldens on the Jews for the privilege of residing in Prague. Despite the persecution, Jewish scholarship in Prague continued to flourish. Among the prominent rabbis in the 18th century were Rabbi Eliyahu Spira, Rabbi Dovid Oppenheim, and the Noda b’Yehuda, Rabbi Yecḥezkel Landau. The Reign of Emperor Josef II and the Edict of Tolerance Whereas Empress Maria Theresa’s view on the Jews was to expel or convert them, her son, Josef II, viewed the Jews as beneficial to the country. He was focused on building the economy and a modern state with the help of the Jews. He also planned to give increased rights to all non-Catholics, with the vision of creating a strong centralized and united country. After his mother died in 1780, Emperor Josef II began implementing his more liberal views. However, there were strong reactions from his populace. Some agreed with the emperor in support of Jewish emancipation. Others vehemently opposed, publishing pamphlets depicting the Jews as traitors who murdered Christians and would eventually destroy the monarchy. In response, Josef II ultimately modified his more ambitious plans. In October 1781, Josef II issued the Edict of Tolerance for the Jews of Bohemia, and in 1782 for Moravian Jewry. Although it was not a declaration of equal rights, the Edict of Tolerance gave Jews their first opportunity to enter the larger world. The Jews appreciated Joseph II so much that they named the Jewish Quarter, Josefov, after him, and this name still exists today. There are several points to stress about the Edict of Tolerance. This was not a Civil Rights Act. Although Josef II boasted that his edict granted the Jews “near-equality,” in truth, this was an exaggeration. The edict did state that Jews no longer had to wear special identifying marks. Yet, the edict continued to deny citizenship to the Jews and forbade them from becoming master craftsmen. The Familiants Law was upheld. Jews continued to be confined to the ghetto until 1849, and complete emancipation would come only in 1867. As part of its goal to integrate the Jews into the state’s economy, the edict set requirements that essentially decreased the Judaism of the Jews. The use of Hebrew in all business documents and secular transactions was forbidden. Universities were open to Jews, and Jews were encouraged to start factories and engage in agriculture, although they were still forbidden to own land. Jews were also strongly encouraged to close their exclusively Jewish schools, and open new schools that included secular studies. The emperor was most candid in his observation that the purpose of the edict was “to make [the Jews] useful to the state.” Subsequent decrees continued to send Jews down the road of integration and assimilation. In 1784, the authority of the beis din (Jewish court of law) was abolished except in religious and marital matters, and disputes were required to be tried in secular courts. In 1786, a law decreed that only graduates of secular elementary schools would be permitted to marry. In 1787, Jews were required to adopt German surnames. With restrictions placed on their Jewish language, education, communal authority, and even names, the Crown felt that Jews would be more integrated and more valuable to the economy of the monarchy. The Impact of the Edict of Tolerance on the Jews From the earliest signs of emancipation, debates have raged about whether the reforms were good for the Jewish community or the beginning of its destruction. On the one hand, the state of constant persecution was devastating. On the other hand, with integration encouraged and demanded from the outside, Jewish identity faced a challenge from which it would never quite recover. Ironically, Jews had survived as a nation and maintained their unique identity and role through 17 centuries of almost unceasing attacks and expulsions. Yet, when the legal barriers that held them back began to disappear, Jews found that the most successful way to enter European society was to abandon their Jewish heritage. The 19th century ushered in an age of assimilation that had no precedent in Jewish history. The greatest rabbi in Bohemia in the 18th century, Rabbi Yechezkel Landau (1713-1793), was elected chief rabbi one year after a catastrophic fire in Prague in 1754. He had succeeded in building the Prague Jewish community into one of the most vibrant Jewish communities in Central Europe. Rabbi Landau foresaw that the Edict of Tolerance would lead the Jews on a path away from the Torah. Despite his concerns, he realized he would have to compromise in the face of the monarchy’s steadfast determination to “educate” the Jews. After he was given a role in planning the schools and was assured that the most radical plans would not be implemented, Rabbi Landau gave the schools his tacit approval The Synagogue of the Jubilee was constructed outside the old Jewish quarter in the Nove Mesto (New City), in 1905-06, celebrating the integration of Jews into Prague society at the beginning of the century. Jewish emancipation was a gradual process. The ghetto was abolished in 1852, and Josefov became a district of Prague. In 1852, Jews were allowed to own property, and in 1859, to own land. Unfortunately, Rabbi Landau’s concerns were well-founded. Most of Prague’s Jews had assimilated in the aftermath of the emancipation decrees. By 1930, Prague had a 30% intermarriage rate, one of the highest in all of Europe. Prague During the Holocaust In the late 1930s, Jewish refugees escaping the Nazis fled to the Prague area from Germany, Austria, and Sudetenland. Whereas in 1930, 35,463 Jews were living in Prague, there were nearly 55,000 Jews there in 1940. Polish Jewish children, many of whom are orphaned, en route to safety in American Zones of Austria and Germany. Prague, Czechoslovakia. c. 1946. (JDC Archives) On March 14, 1939, Slovakia declared independence from Prague and signed the Treaty of Protection with Nazi Germany. The next day, Germany occupied the Czech lands. At the outbreak of World War II, Prague was one of the largest Jewish communities in Europe. At the end of the war, two-thirds of the Jewish population of Prague had been murdered in the Holocaust. Over 97,000 Czech Jews perished in the Holocaust, of which 15,000 were Czech Jewish children. Despite the destruction wrought by the Nazis on the Jews and their community, much of Prague’s Jewish architecture remains. How did these buildings of the Jewish Quarter manage to survive? It is believed that Hitler wanted to establish a “Museum of an Extinct Race” in Prague once the war was over. He had hundreds of thousands of Jewish artifacts transported to Prague from all over Europe. Post-World War II In 1945, the Communist Party took power, and in the coming decades, Jewish life was stifled, and emigration to Israel was forbidden as of 1949. Jews who remained in Prague kept their Jewish identity a secret. In 1968, a Slovak Communist named Alexander Dubcek became the party leader. During the Prague Spring, he began introducing sweeping reforms to make the government more democratic. He ordered an end to censorship and encouraged open discussion about the political direction of Czechoslovakia. Many young Jews were involved in the events of the Prague Spring. Additionally, for the first time since World War II, they were able to openly ask questions about the Holocaust and their Jewish heritage. The Soviet Union disapproved of these changes and invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968. Civilians were shot dead in the street, and 3,400 Jews fled the country. The secret police kept a close eye on the remaining Jewish community, and many Jewish university professors lost their jobs. From 1968 to 1989, the Holocaust was forbidden to be mentioned, and survivors were required to be silent on the topic. The End of Communism and a New Reality When change began to sweep through Eastern Europe in the late 1980s, Czechs joined the movement. Demonstrations led to the resignation of the Communist Party leadership in November 1989. Alexander Dubcek, the Prague Spring reformer, was elected chairman of parliament. In June 1990, the country held its first free election since 1946. On January 1, 1993, the country split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia. Prague was adopted as the capital of the Czech Republic. Today, the Federation of Jewish Communities estimates that there are between 3,000 and 5,000 Jews in the Czech Republic, of which 1,600 live in Prague. The beauty of Prague’s Jewish buildings and the old ghetto remain visited by countless tourists. Sadly, Prague, which had been, for a time, the most vibrant, influential and populous Jewish city in the world, has essentially become a museum of testimony to its earlier greatness. Yet, the works produced/ and the Torah taught by its great leaders continue to live on for eternity. They are Jewish Prague’s legacy. Rabbi Menachem Levine is the CEO of JDBY-YTT, the largest Jewish school in the Midwest. He served as Rabbi of Congregation Am Echad in San Jose, CA, from 2007 to 2020. He is a popular speaker and writes for numerous publications on Torah, Jewish History, and Contemporary Jewish Topics. What we know on day 1,647 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Thu 27 Aug 2026 21.12 EDT Last modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 21.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Ukrainian military said it shot down seven ballistic missiles and 258 drones as Russia carried out a lengthy attack that extended over Wednesday night and well into Thursday. “Overnight, Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukraine, targeting ports, grain storage, energy, industry and other infrastructure with ballistic ⁠and hypersonic missiles and combat drones,” said the foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha. Commuters went to work in Kyiv to the boom of air defences firing at waves of ⁠drones, Reuters reported. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week ‌that Kyiv had received a small ‌batch of US-made Patriot interceptors that can shoot down ballistic missiles. In Kharkiv, one person was killed and two were injured in a lunchtime attack on a shopping centre, said the regional governor, Oleh Syniehubov. The strikes also targeted a Kyiv-area retail distribution centre and a shipment hub for a toy company, their ⁠chief executives said. Chocolate firm Roshen, founded by former president Petro Poroshenko, ​said one of its warehouses outside Kyiv was ​destroyed. Russian strikes also hit industrial sites, energy facilities and other infrastructure in the central Poltava and southern Odesa regions, as well as the south-eastern city of ​Kryvyi Rih , officials said. A ⁠Russian attack on a thermal ⁠power plant ⁠in Ukraine’s ​southern city of Kherson ⁠resulted in the loss of ⁠all of its ​generating ‌capacity, state ‌oil and gas company ‌Naftogaz said. “The Russians struck a purely civilian facility that provides heat to ‌a significant portion of Kherson’s ​residential buildings,” said the company’s CEO, Sergiy Fedorenko. The Kherson regional governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, called for people to leave the city if they could, “especially families with children and elderly people”. “Last night, Russian forces again attacked Kherson’s district heating plant with glide bombs … the facility sustained very serious damage. Kherson may find itself without electricity or heating not for hours or days but for a long period.” Six Russian drones crossed into the airspace of Ukraine’s neighbour Moldova , local authorities said, prompting the president, Maia Sandu, to “strongly condemn this intimidation”. One of them was found on Moldovan territory. A Russian serviceman was killed by a car bomb in St Petersburg on Thursday , officials said. His wife was injured. Throughout the war, assassinations have targeted key Russian military personnel, military-industrial figures and prominent supporters of the war effort – both within Russia and in occupied Ukraine. Kyiv’s security services including the SBU have claimed responsibility for some of the killings. The Guardian’s Peter Beaumont has written about how far Russia is having to go to import diesel and gasoline because of the damage Ukrainian strikes have done to its petroleum industry . So many refineries are damaged that Russian oil is being sent to Kazakhstan for processing into fuels that are shipped back . For the first time, Russia this week bought 200,000 barrels of gasoline from Turkey – the fifth confirmed seaborne delivery of vehicle fuel this summer, after previous shipments from India amounting to 1m barrels in total. Ukraine’s drone attacks have left Russia desperately scrambling for oil imports Read more “In the space of a summer,” Peter Beaumont writes, “Russia, once the world’s second-largest producer of crude oil , has been plunged into a desperate scramble to find sources of gasoline to plug the ever-growing holes in its refining capacity.” Russia has signed a deal with the Kondensat oil refinery in western Kazakhstan this week to process Russian crude, with 70% of the refined fuel shipped back to Russia – by rail according to reports, because there is no pipeline. Fuel imports from war ally Belarus this June increased by a factor of 141 compared with June 2025. The Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden called on Thursday for the EU to look again at using frozen Russian central bank assets to finance Ukraine . The four countries have told the EU executive in a letter: “We believe now is the time to revert to the issue of how we can make further use of Russia’s immobilised assets for the benefit of Ukraine.” The EU has failed to strike a deal on tapping the roughly €200bn (£170bn/US$230bn) after objections from Belgium, where the vast bulk of the financial assets are held, that it could be deemed legally liable. EU countries instead loaned Ukraine €90bn. An ⁠arson attack planned by three suspects in eastern Slovakia targeted drone maker Skyeton , prosecutors said on Thursday. Skyeton, founded in Ukraine, says it produces drones for civilian and military use in Ukraine and other countries. “The attack was ⁠supposed to aim at the Skyeton company’s factory,” said a spokesperson for the regional prosecutor’s office in the eastern city of Presov. A German prosecutor told ​Reuters that a 26-year-old Latvian had ‌been detained in Hamburg ‌and extradition proceedings were under way. Slovak prosecutors said a ‌Latvian and a Ukrainian had been detained in Slovakia. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Veronica Escobar, who represents Texas’s 16th congressional district, said of her oversight attempts: ‘It’s been very challenging at times.’ Photograph: Michael Brochstein/SOPA Images/REX/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Veronica Escobar, who represents Texas’s 16th congressional district, said of her oversight attempts: ‘It’s been very challenging at times.’ Photograph: Michael Brochstein/SOPA Images/REX/Shutterstock ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Democrat says ICE blocked her oversight visit to country’s largest detention camp Veronica Escobar tells Guardian she was prevented from speaking to detainees at much-criticized Texas facility José Olivares Tue 22 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Federal immigration officials in Texas prevented US representative Veronica Escobar from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) detention center, the lawmaker said in an interview with the Guardian. Escobar, a Democrat who represents El Paso and surrounding areas on the US-Mexico border in west Texas, conducted an oversight visit last month at the Camp East Montana ICE tent facility housed in the Fort Bliss military base, after two separate “disturbances” had been reported there in recent weeks. But when she arrived to scrutinize conditions at the camp, the largest ICE detention center in the country, she said she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants. She also requested surveillance footage of the reported incidents but said she has not received it. “The administration obviously has attempted to block congressional oversight,” Escobar said in a telephone interview with the Guardian. “It’s been very challenging at times. And that has depended on, to a large extent, what the directive has been from the administration.” The constraints placed on Escobar is one of the latest instances in which the Trump administration has limited members of Congress’s ability to conduct oversight visits into federal immigration detention centers. Escobar and other federal lawmakers sued the Trump administration last year for blocking such access. Despite a federal judge ruling in favor of the lawmakers last December, there have been subsequent reports of ICE officials placing limits on or turning away members of congress when attempting to conduct oversight visits. “Oversight, during the second Trump administration, has certainly been significantly more challenging than during the first Trump administration,” Escobar added. Camp East Montana was hastily constructed last summer at the huge army base in El Paso. Unlike other ICE detention centers housed in buildings, this facility is a sprawling “soft-sided” tent camp. It has the capacity to hold up to 5,000 people and has drawn complaints and demands for its closure from the time it opened. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, reported two separate “disturbances” within one week there in early September. On 1 September, it alleged that detained immigrants assaulted security staff by striking, kicking and throwing tablets at them. On 7 September, a larger group of around 130 detained immigrants allegedly threw items, flipped furniture and disabled security cameras. The detainees also knocked down partitions between the tented living quarters, known as pods, at the detention camp, Escobar said. An ICE official at the facility called 911 during the incident, according to reporting by the El Paso Times. The newspaper’s revelation contradicted what ICE officials apparently told Escobar during her visit . View image in fullscreen A sign marks the entrance to the Camp East Montana immigrant detention center. Photograph: Morgan Lee/AP “While there absolutely have been serious issues and mismanagement, fraud, deaths, and a homicide, there had never been a riot,” Escobar said. “There had never been, especially in two weeks in a row, situations where the contractor lost control of the population in their custody.” Escobar said that when she spoke with an ICE official about incidents, the official pointed to the detained immigrants’ nationality as the cause. “The deputy was very quick to blame the nationality of the detainees, saying that the Venezuelans are a difficult population,” Escobar said. It is still unclear what exactly happened during the two incidents. Members of Congress have the legal power to conduct oversight visits into ICE detention facilities nationwide, by visiting the sites without prior notice and speaking with detained immigrants. Lawmakers have claimed that the Trump administration has limited those oversight visits by requiring lawmakers to submit the names and personal information of detainees they want to speak with beforehand. The homeland security department disputed Escobar’s claims in an email to the Guardian, while adding that it considers many oversight visits “a media act”, and also denied that there has been an official request for data and footage. “Any member of Congress can still request to speak with any illegal alien in ICE custody,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “If an illegal alien and a member of Congress agree to meet with one another, ICE will facilitate the meeting. We are not stopping members of Congress from meeting with illegal aliens, including many with criminal histories in ICE custody, or touring ICE facilities.” Since Camp East Montana opened last summer, it has been plagued with accusations of abuse, mismanagement and dire conditions. Immigrants and human rights groups have repeatedly alleged human rights and constitutional violations at the site, including physical abuse, sexual harassment, inedible food and medical neglect. ICE was sued over alleged “dire” conditions earlier this year. ‘Dire’ conditions at ICE facility severely violate human rights, lawsuit claims Read more At least three people detained at the site have died in ICE custody, including a 55-year-old man whose January death was ruled a homicide after security guards beat him. This year, an internal ICE inspection found a number of deficiencies at the site, including with guards’ use of force. A US government accountability office report also found a series of problems with the facility’s contract, its construction and the conditions. The office made four recommendations to DHS, ICE and the US army. Those recommendations remain “open”, meaning they have not been resolved. “That facility, from my perspective, should not be operational,” Escobar said. “It should have been shut down a long time ago.” During her recent Camp East Montana oversight visit, Escobar pressed for the private contractor running the facility to be held accountable for the recent incidents, not just the detained immigrants deemed responsible. Earlier this year, ICE gave the multi-million-dollar contract for running the facility on its behalf to a new private security company. View image in fullscreen Protesters opposing mass deportations by ICE hold signs during a rally outside Fort Bliss. Photograph: Paul Ratje/Reuters “The contractor needs to eat those costs [of the damage]. If they were not prepared, if they were unable to control the situation, the American taxpayer should not pay for their incompetence,” Escobar said. “These private contractors are making enormous sums of money. And frankly, there needed to be accountability with this contractor.” The DHS spokesman said that far from closing, Camp East Montana “is upgrading” and claimed that the contractor now running the site was providing more services and “precise quality assurance”. “ICE is always looking at ways to improve our detention facilities to ensure we are providing the best care to illegal aliens in our custody,” the spokesperson said. Amentum Services, a Maryland-based contractor now running the Camp East Montana facility, did not respond to a request for comment. Acquisition Logistics, a small and relatively-unknown company based in Virginia first secured a nearly $1.3bn contract to run the site. Amentum took over this April after previously working as a subcontractor at the site. Meanwhile, there have been further accusations of alleged rights violations at other detention facilities. The Guardian has reported exclusively on a series of force feedings in ICE facilities, including inside two detention centers in Texas . During the first Trump administration, Escobar criticized and investigated ICE’s use of force feeding on hunger strikers in 2019 . “It’s a very barbaric practice,” Escobar said. “The rapid expansion of immigration detention, under the [second] Trump administration– and fueled by Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill – it is allowing more and more of this absolutely unacceptable behavior by the federal government to continue.” Explore more on these topics ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Democrats US politics Trump administration US immigration news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
